symptom_description: First noticeable symptoms develop on leaf blades and consist of small chlorotic spots, arranged as alternate bands of diseased and healthy tissue. Spots on the mid-ribs are circular and dark brown, while lesions on the laminae continue as chlorotic spots. Nodes and internodes also show brown lesions. In severe infections, these may coalesce and induce stalk rotting and lodging.
trigger_conditions: Normally the disease occurs in areas of abundant rainfall and high mean temperatures.

common_name: Crazy Top Downy Mildew / Yellow Wilt of Rice
symptom_description: Usually, there is chlorotic striping of leaves and leaf sheaths, and dwarfing. Induces tassel malformations where no pollen is produced, and ears, if formed at all, are nubbins. Leaves may be narrow, thick, and abnormally erect.
trigger_conditions: The disease is most prevalent in warm and humid regions.
disambiguation_notes: False head smut does not produce tassel malformation or ear infection as does true head smut (Sphacelotheca reiliana).

symptom_description: Chlorotic striping of leaves and leaf sheaths, and dwarfing. Conspicuous after development of a 'downy growth' on or under leaf surfaces.
trigger_conditions: The disease is most prevalent in warm and humid regions.

common_name: Graminicola Downy Mildew of Maize / Green Ear Disease
symptom_description: Chlorotic striping of leaves and leaf sheaths, and dwarfing. Conspicuous downy growth on or under leaf surfaces.
trigger_conditions: Prevalent in warm and humid regions.

symptom_description: Chlorotic striping of leaves and leaf sheaths, and dwarfing.
trigger_conditions: Prevalent in warm and humid regions.

symptom_description: Chlorotic striping of leaves and leaf sheaths, and dwarfing. Conspicuous downy growth on or under leaf surfaces.
trigger_conditions: Prevalent in warm and humid regions.

symptom_description: Chlorotic striping of leaves and leaf sheaths, and dwarfing.
trigger_conditions: Prevalent in warm and humid regions.

symptom_description: Chlorotic striping of leaves and leaf sheaths, and dwarfing. Downy growth on or under leaf surfaces, most conspicuous after conidia formation which commonly occurs in early morning.
trigger_conditions: Prevalent in warm and humid regions.

symptom_description: Characteristic black, raised and shiny spots are produced early. At a later stage, necrotic areas develop around the 'tar spot'. These necrotic lesions may coalesce and cause a complete burning of the foliage. Lesions start developing before tasseling time on lower leaves, moving upwards on younger leaves. Affected ears are light weight.
trigger_conditions: Sometimes occurs in relatively cool, humid areas of the tropics, where Turcicum leaf blight is prevalent.

symptom_description: Characterized by elongate raised bumps (pustules) scattered or clustered together on both leaf surfaces that are red to dark brown in color. The symptoms are mainly observed in the mid and upper canopy of the crop in stage II and III of crop development. These occur most conspicuously when plants approach tasseling. Later the epidermis is ruptured and the lesions turn black and spores are released as the plant matures.
trigger_conditions: Disease spread is favored by humid warm conditions and in severe cases cause death of the leaves.
disambiguation_notes: Southern rust pustules are small, round, light orange, later turning black. Tropical rust pustules are small, round-to-oval, surrounded by black epidermis.
recommended_action: Grow resistant varieties, control alternate hosts (Wood sorrel / Oxalis spp.) and spray with fungicides.
confidence_source: CIMMYT Maize Diseases Guide p. 13; KALRO Disease Guide p. 22; KCEP-CRAL Maize Extension Manual p. 11

symptom_description: Pustules are small, round, light orange; later turning black. The epidermis is ruptured as the plant matures.
trigger_conditions: Favored by humid warm conditions.
disambiguation_notes: Differs from common rust in that southern rust pustules are lighter orange, smaller, and rounder.
recommended_action: Foliar application of fungicides.

symptom_description: Pustules are small, round-to-oval, surrounded by black epidermis.
trigger_conditions: Prevalent in warm and humid tropical regions.
disambiguation_notes: Differs from common and southern rust in that the pustules are surrounded by a distinct black epidermis.

symptom_description: Large, concentric, necrotic rings on the leaves.
trigger_conditions: Favored by cool, humid conditions.

symptom_description: Small, necrotic lesions coalescing into concentric necrotic spots.
trigger_conditions: Prevalent in humid, warm tropical environments.

symptom_description: Small, round-to-oval spots, pale green, later becoming bleached, then necrotic with a dark brown margin.
trigger_conditions: Prevalent in humid, cool regions.
disambiguation_notes: Other species of Leptosphaerta which produce different symptoms on maize leaves are also known in other regions of the world.

symptom_description: Lesions begin as small, regular, elongated brown-gray necrotic spots growing parallel to the veins. Mature lesions are oval in shape and occasionally, lesions may reach 5cm long and 0.3 cm wide. The lesions start from the lower leaves and increase in number usually after 'silking' in stage III of plant development. They are always light and develop into gray lesions which may grow together and kill entire leaves.
likely_cause: Cercospora zeae-maydis / Cercospora sorghi var. maydis
trigger_conditions: Develops in highly humid warm, overcast days. Minimum tillage practices have been associated with an increased incidence of GLS.
disambiguation_notes: Cigar-shaped lesions are characteristic of Northern Corn Leaf Blight, whereas Gray Leaf Spot lesions are strictly restricted parallel to the leaf veins.
recommended_action: Plough under diseased debris to reduce amount of inoculum, plant resistant/tolerant varieties, practice crop rotation for at least 2 years with non-host crops like potato, beans or pea, use recommended rates of fertilizers and spray with fungicides.
confidence_source: CIMMYT Maize Diseases Guide p. 22; KALRO Disease Guide p. 21; KCEP-CRAL Maize Extension Manual p. 11

symptom_description: Lesions, with brown centers, about 2 mm in diameter. Spots are small and necrotic, with light colored haloes.
likely_cause: Curvularia clavata / Curvularia maculans / Curvularia pallescens / Curvularia senegalensis / Curvularia tuberculata / Curvularia lunata
trigger_conditions: Prevalent in warm, humid tropical environments.
disambiguation_notes: Easily confused with eyespot of maize or physiological/genetical spots.

symptom_description: Lesions are oval, zonate, and brownish, or brown slender and elongated. Can cause rotten and blackened ears.
trigger_conditions: Prevalent in humid, warm conditions.

common_name: Maydis Leaf Blight / Southern Corn Leaf Blight
symptom_description: Lesions are small, elongating along secondary veins, and often coalescing. Lesions are oval and larger than 2.3 cm on husks and leaf sheaths in specific strains.
trigger_conditions: Humid, warm weather favors disease development.
disambiguation_notes: Southern leaf blight spots are restricted by leaf veins at first, up to 25 mm long, whereas Northern leaf blight spots are cigar-shaped and larger.
recommended_action: Use disease-free seed or treated seed, destroy crop residues and volunteer plants, practice crop rotation, and use tolerant/resistant varieties.
confidence_source: CIMMYT Maize Diseases Guide p. 29; KCEP-CRAL Maize Extension Manual p. 11

common_name: Turcicum Leaf Blight / Northern Corn Leaf Blight (NLB)
symptom_description: Early symptoms include chlorotic 'halo' that develop into necrotic lesions. These grow into mature cigar-shaped lesions that are 2 cm wide and about 15 cm long. Immature lesions have gray green margins and as they mature turn brown with dark parts of fungal sporulation. The symptoms appear first on lower leaves and increase in size and number as the plant develops, until foliage is completely 'burned'.
likely_cause: Helminthosporium turcicum / Exserohilum turcicum / Exhelosporium turcicum
trigger_conditions: Favored by cool, wet weather and is aggravated by previous diseased leaf tissue left on the soil surface.
disambiguation_notes: Turcicum leaf blight lesions are large and cigar-shaped, distinguishing them from the rectangular lesions of Gray Leaf Spot and the smaller spots of Southern Leaf Blight.
recommended_action: Ploughing in or removal of the diseased leaf materials from the soil surface, planting resistant/tolerant varieties, crop rotation, and spraying with fungicides before the disease becomes severe.
confidence_source: CIMMYT Maize Diseases Guide p. 30; KALRO Disease Guide p. 20; KCEP-CRAL Maize Extension Manual p. 11
region_notes: The purpose of this section is to help with recognition of the common diseases of maize in Kenya caused by infectious pathogens such as fungi, bacteria, viruses and nematodes.

symptom_description: Lesions are necrotic, elongated, with narrow yellow margins, along the leaf veins.
trigger_conditions: Prevalent in warm, humid conditions.

symptom_description: Lesions coalesce and produce severe blotching and necrosis of leaf tissue. Stalks of young plants may also be infected.
trigger_conditions: Favored by warm, wet environments.

symptom_description: Symptoms first appear as small, light green to yellow spots on the leaves. Lesions coalesce and produce severe blotching and necrosis of affected areas where many black pycnidia grow.
trigger_conditions: The spotting mainly affects maize grown in rather cool, humid environments.

symptom_description: Recognized by small (1 to 4 mm), round, translucent lesions. Tan colored centers develop, surrounded by black-to-purple rings, with a yellow halo around them, thus producing the characteristic 'eyespot'.
trigger_conditions: Favored by cool, moist environments.
disambiguation_notes: These symptoms are easily confused with physiological or genetical spots, which are non-infectious but widely observed in maize leaves.

common_name: Phyllosticta Leaf Spot / Yellow Leaf Blight
symptom_description: Young diseased plants show symptoms similar to those observed in nitrogen deficient plants. In mature plants, lesions are narrow, necrotic, and parallel to the veins (although not limited by them). In older leaves, lesions develop further and produce a characteristic blighting near the tip.
trigger_conditions: Humid, warm weather favors disease development.
disambiguation_notes: Young plant symptoms look similar to nitrogen deficiency.

symptom_description: Concentric spots on leaves and sheaths; filamentous masses develop on lesions. Rotten ears; light brown cottony mold: filamentous masses on kernels and cob.
trigger_conditions: Prevalent in warm, humid conditions.

symptom_description: Twisting and collapsing of the stalk. Affected internodes show a dark, water-soaked, soft rot. Stalks of young plants collapse.
trigger_conditions: Favored by hot, wet weather.
confidence_source: CIMMYT Maize Diseases Guide p. 45; KALRO Disease Guide p. 26
region_notes: Pl ease note that this disease has not yet been reported in Kenya and is therefore of quarantine importance.

symptom_description: The infection is systemic: the fungus penetrates the seedlings and grows inside the plant without showing symptoms, until the tasseling and silking in stage II and III of crop development. The most conspicuous symptoms are: abnormal development of the tassels, which become malformed and overgrown; black masses of spores that develop inside individual male florets; and masses of black spores replacing the normal ear, leaving the vascular bundles exposed and shredded looking like fibers. Plants may be severely stunted.
trigger_conditions: Can cause significant economic damage in dry, hot maize growing areas, and in mid hill zones and under warm temperate conditions.
disambiguation_notes: It is different from common smut for lack of the vascular bundles that appear as fiber in smut-infected ears.
recommended_action: Plant resistant varieties, plant early when temperatures are unfavorable for spore germination, treat seeds with systemic fungicides, maintain balanced soil fertility, remove and burn smutted tassels and ears as they emerge, and practice crop rotation.
confidence_source: CIMMYT Maize Diseases Guide p. 46; KALRO Disease Guide p. 23; KCEP-CRAL Maize Extension Manual p. 12

symptom_description: Brown interior of the stem, starting in the roots; wilting of the plant at flowering. Stunting; chlorosis; death around flowering time. Nubbins, or ears with underdeveloped, shrunken kernels.
trigger_conditions: Systemic infection starting early and showing symptoms at flowering.
recommended_action: Practice crop rotation and use healthy seeds.
confidence_source: CIMMYT Maize Diseases Guide p. 49; KALRO Disease Guide p. 8
region_notes: f) Resource mobilization The technical team held several consultative forums to share information and develop a research proposal for sustainab le management of MLND in Kenya.

symptom_description: Rapid wilting of leaves and stalks at or near flowering. Stem interior shows a brown discoloration.
trigger_conditions: Favored by warm temperatures.

symptom_description: Black discoloration of stem; shredding of interior; bundles of black material. Split stalks show vascular bundles covered with black, pin-head-like sclerotia.
trigger_conditions: Favored by dry weather and high temperatures.
disambiguation_notes: Unlike charcoal rot, Botryodiplodia stalk rot does not produce black pin-head-like sclerotia in the rotten areas, but it does produce abundant gray-blackish cottony mycelium.

symptom_description: Only a few isolated male florets in the tassel show dark-green masses of spores (sori). Does not produce tassel malformation or ear infection.
trigger_conditions: Occurs very rarely in hot, dry or humid areas.
disambiguation_notes: Differs from True Head Smut in that it does not cause tassel malformation or ear infection. Differs from Common Smut in that no galls are produced.

common_name: Botryodiplodia Stalk Rot / Black Kernel Rot
symptom_description: Diseased plants dry prematurely. Split-open stalks show some shredding of the pith and a dark gray to black discoloration of the vascular bundles. Abundant grayish mycelia are conspicuous in the rotten areas, confined mostly to the lower internodes above ground. Produces abundant gray-blackish cottony mycelium in cavities formed in the pith of affected internodes.
trigger_conditions: Develops in hot, humid environments.
disambiguation_notes: Unlike charcoal rot, Botryodiplodia stalk rot does not produce black pin-head-like sclerotia in the rotten areas.

symptom_description: Broken stalks; brownish pith; later, abundant-fruiting bodies. Rotting starts at the base.
trigger_conditions: Favored by wet weather after flowering.

symptom_description: Damage occurs mainly on individual kernels or on limited areas of the ear. Infected kernels develop a cottony growth or may develop white streaks on the pericarp and germinate on the cob. Scattered individual or groups of kernels show whitish-pink to lavender fungal growth. Infected kernels may also have a 'starburst' pattern of white streaks on the cap of the kernel or along the base.
trigger_conditions: Infections are more frequent on damaged ear tips, and are favored by dry weather. Mechanical damage by thrips to developing kernels provides entry.
disambiguation_notes: In contrast to Gibberella zeae which covers the ear starting from the tip with reddish mycelium, Fusarium moniliforme damage occurs mainly on individual kernels.
recommended_action: Avoid injuring the plants. Spray with fungicides.
confidence_source: CIMMYT Maize Diseases Guide p. 64; KALRO Disease Guide p. 25

symptom_description: Gibberella zeae produces reddish kernel discoloration, usually beginning at the ear tip. Ear infection begins as white mycelium moving down from the tip, which later turns reddish-pink, in infected kernels. Husks may rot and be cemented to the ear.
trigger_conditions: Most common in cool and humid weather, particularly 2 to 3 weeks after silking.
disambiguation_notes: Gibberella ear rot causes a distinct reddish-pink discoloration moving down from the tip, whereas Aspergillus causes black or green-yellow powdery masses.
confidence_source: CIMMYT Maize Diseases Guide p. 64, 68; KALRO Disease Guide p. 25

symptom_description: Inner parts of the ear show black discoloration. Pith is shredded and black.
trigger_conditions: Favored by hot, dry conditions.

symptom_description: Slimy, soft, pale, masses develop on kernels; these harden toward harvest and turn dark.
trigger_conditions: Favored by cool, humid climates.

symptom_description: Blue-green powdery mold on the cob and kernels; kernels appear streaked and bleached.
trigger_conditions: Favored by ear injury.

symptom_description: Produces black, powdery masses of spores that cover both kernels and cob (for Aspergillus niger). Greenish or yellowish-tan discoloration occurs on and between kernels, especially near the ear tip. Symptoms are more prevalent if the husk does not cover the ear tip in stage II of crop development.
trigger_conditions: The rot is favored by hot, dry weather. May be a serious problem when infected ears are stored at high moisture content.
disambiguation_notes: Aspergillus produces green, yellow, or black powdery spores, unlike the white mold of Diplodia or the reddish-pink growth of Gibberella.
recommended_action: Dry maize grain quickly after harvest to moisture levels of between 12 and 15% and ensure good ventilation. Avoid ear damage by birds or insects.
confidence_source: CIMMYT Maize Diseases Guide p. 76; KALRO Disease Guide p. 24

symptom_description: Lightweight, chaffy ears; loose, discolored kernels; black specks on kernels and cob. Germination of seed on cob can occur.
trigger_conditions: Favored by warm, wet weather.

symptom_description: Characterized by galls that replace individual kernels and are covered with white membranes. In time the galls break open releasing black masses of spores that will infect maize in the following season. On the leaves the disease appears as white blisters that turn dark with age. The blisters tend to harden and dry without rupturing. The disease is most severe in young plants and can stunt or kill them. Attacks all parts of the plant: leaves, stalks, tassels and ears.
trigger_conditions: Occurs mainly in the humid and temperate areas as opposed to hot humid tropical areas. The pathogen survives in soils as teliospores in a wide range of temperatures (16-35oC). Entry is gained through wounds or thin walled cells of actively growing maize.
disambiguation_notes: It is different from head smut for lack of the vascular bundles that appear as fiber in smut-infected ears.
recommended_action: Burn affected plants completely, plant resistant varieties, spray with fungicides, and avoid injuring the plants.
confidence_source: CIMMYT Maize Diseases Guide p. 80; KALRO Disease Guide p. 22; KCEP-CRAL Maize Extension Manual p. 12

symptom_description: Lightweight, chaffy ears; loose, discolored kernels; black specks on kernels and cob.
trigger_conditions: Favored by cool, wet conditions.

symptom_description: Brown-green streaks on kernels, starting at the cob base.
trigger_conditions: Favored by wet weather and crop lodging.

symptom_description: Symptoms include bleached husks, white mold over kernels, and rotted ears with tightly adhering husks. Early infection (2 to 4 weeks after silking) is likely to lead to complete ear rotting. Later infections may result in partial rotting, usually beginning at the base.
trigger_conditions: Most severe when maize is planted following corn in reduced tillage situations. Most ear rots are favored by late-season humidity and ear damage.
disambiguation_notes: Characterized by white mycelial growth that tightly glues husks to the ear, which distinguishes it from the pinkish/reddish Gibberella ear rot.
recommended_action: Crop rotation, deep tillage, and avoid planting maize immediately following maize in fields with a history of the disease.
confidence_source: CIMMYT Maize Diseases Guide p. 87; KALRO Disease Guide p. 24

symptom_description: Affected plants show a rapid wilting, followed by collapse and lodging of the stalk. Internodes show a dark, water-soaked, soft, slimy rot that has a foul odor.
trigger_conditions: Favored by high temperatures and abundant rainfall or overhead irrigation.
disambiguation_notes: Bacterial stalk rot is distinguished by its slimy, soft rot with a characteristic foul odor.
recommended_action: Avoid overhead irrigation, improve soil drainage, and spray with recommended bactericides.
confidence_source: CIMMYT Maize Diseases Guide p. 88; KALRO Disease Guide p. 26
region_notes: Pl ease note that this disease has not yet been reported in Kenya and is therefore of quarantine importance.

symptom_description: With early infection, lesions are first water-soaked, turning long and pale yellow with irregular margins running the length of the leaves. Infection may move into the stem, causing a general stunting, wilting, and plant death. Severely infected plants that set seed develop small nubbins with few kernels. Late infection can cause severe leaf necrosis but does not lead to wilting.
trigger_conditions: Transmitted by maize flea beetles (Chaetocnema pulicaria) and also at very low frequency through infected seed. Feeding wounds from the insect vector serve as points of entry.
disambiguation_notes: Stewart's wilt causes long, water-soaked, pale yellow leaf lesions, unlike the rectangular lesions of gray leaf spot.
recommended_action: Quarantine measures (not yet reported in Kenya), control the flea beetle vector, plant resistant varieties.
confidence_source: CIMMYT Maize Diseases Guide p. 91; KALRO Disease Guide p. 26
region_notes: Not yet reported in Kenya (quarantine importance).

symptom_description: Lesions are pale green along the veins, later becoming bleached and necrotic.
trigger_conditions: Favored by warm, wet conditions.

symptom_description: Lesions start as water-soaked spots, later turning round, light-colored or white with reddish margins.
trigger_conditions: Favored by cool, wet weather.
region_notes: Pl ease note that this disease has not yet been reported in Kenya and is therefore of quarantine importance.

symptom_description: Bushy plant; many tillers, chlorotic and reddish; severe stunting.
trigger_conditions: Transmitted by leafhopper vectors.
disambiguation_notes: Maize bushy stunt causes excessive tillering and a bushy appearance, which is more pronounced than the symptoms of corn stunt.
recommended_action: Control leafhopper vectors, plant early, and use resistant varieties.

symptom_description: Stunting; chlorosis; shortened internodes; leaves appear crowded.
trigger_conditions: Transmitted by leafhopper vectors.
recommended_action: Control vectors.

symptom_description: Stunting; chlorosis; shortened internodes; green patches. Underdeveloped ears and poor grain filling. Usually associated with mosaic pattern and chlorotic streaks on leaves.
trigger_conditions: Transmitted by rootworm beetles, thrips, aphids and leafhoppers. Also has low levels of seed transmission. The virus is geographically restricted and is associated with soil.
disambiguation_notes: Co-infection of MCMV with potyviruses (SCMV or MDMV) leads to the devastating Maize Lethal Necrosis Disease (MLND).
recommended_action: Control vectors, plant early, use certified seeds, crop rotation.
confidence_source: CIMMYT Maize Diseases Guide p. 99; KALRO Disease Guide p. 8, 14
region_notes: Reported in Bomet, Narok, Naivasha, Nakuru counties.

symptom_description: Infected plants develop a distinct mosaic — irregularities in the distribution of normal green color —on the youngest leaf bases. Sometimes the mosaic appearance is enhanced by narrow chlorotic streaks extending parallel to the veins. Later on, the youngest leaves show a general chlorosis, and streaks are larger and more abundant. As plants approach maturity, the foliage can turn purple or purple-red. Depending on time of infection, there may be severe stunting of the plant. Plants infected early may produce nubbins or be totally barren.
trigger_conditions: Transmitted by several genera and species of aphids, including Rhopalosiphum maidis, and also by seed at low rates. Can infect other grass and cereal hosts like sorghum, Johnson grass, and sugarcane.
disambiguation_notes: mosaic patterns and chlorotic streaks distinguish it from Maize Streak Virus, which has sharp, broken yellow lines.
recommended_action: Control aphid vectors, plant early, use resistant varieties, eradicate alternate grass hosts.
confidence_source: CIMMYT Maize Diseases Guide p. 100; KALRO Disease Guide p. 7, 28
region_notes: b) History of MLND in Kenya In K enya the first occurrence of unfamiliar maize disease was first reported in September 2011 in the low altitude zones of Bomet County (Longisa Division, 1900.

symptom_description: Infected plants show a diverse range of symptoms. These include chlorotic mottle on the leaves, usually starting from the base of the young leaves in the whorl and extending upwards toward the leaf tips, mild to severe leaf mottling, dwarfing and premature aging. Necrosis of the young leaves in the whorl before expansion leading to a 'dead heart'. Lesions sometimes associated with unfurled leaves appear on the stem. Tassels with no pollen and finally there is poor grain filing.
trigger_conditions: Involves synergism between two viruses: MCMV and any of several potyviruses (SCMV, MDMV, WSMV). Transmitted by rootworm beetles, thrips, aphids and leafhoppers. Alternate hosts include a wide range of plants in the grass family (73 species). Low levels of seed transmission.
disambiguation_notes: MLN is characterized by rapid and complete drying of the plant (necrosis), leading to a 'dead heart', which is much more severe than the mosaic symptoms of MDMV or MCMV alone.
recommended_action: Integrated pest and disease management: plant early, use certified treated seeds with insecticide, avoid recycled seeds, crop rotation with non-cereal crops (beans, cowpeas, peas), crop diversification, closed seasons (quarantine on movement of materials), control insect vectors (thrips, aphids) using recommended chemical or biological agents.
confidence_source: CIMMYT Maize Diseases Guide p. 103; KALRO Disease Guide p. 10, 14, 15, 16; KCEP-CRAL Maize Extension Manual p. 12
region_notes: First reported in September 2011 in low altitude zones of Bomet County (Longisa Division). Spread to Narok South, Narok North, Naivasha, Nakuru, Nandi, Bungoma, Kakamega sub-counties. Present in all maize growing regions except North Eastern.

symptom_description: Chlorotic striping; leaves appear crowded and erect; leaves rough, fleshy, dark purple.
trigger_conditions: Transmitted by planthopper vectors.
recommended_action: Control vectors.

symptom_description: Yellow and broad striping, turning purple toward leaf tips.
trigger_conditions: Transmitted by planthopper vectors.
recommended_action: Control vectors.

symptom_description: Spots, small and whitish, coalescing into a line. Fine chlorotic spots parallel to the veins.
trigger_conditions: Transmitted by leafhopper vectors.
recommended_action: Control vectors.

symptom_description: Early disease symptoms begin within a week after infection and consist of very small, round, scattered spots in the youngest leaves. The number of spots increases with plant growth; they enlarge parallel to the leaf veins. Soon spots become more profuse at leaf bases. Fully elongated leaves develop a chlorosis with broken yellow streaks along the veins, contrasting with the dark green color of normal foliage. Severe infection causes stunting, and plants can die prematurely or are barren.
trigger_conditions: Transmitted by Cicadulina spp. leafhoppers (primarily Cicadulina mbila). Alternate hosts include many cereal crops and wild grasses. Early planting reduces risk of virus transmission.
disambiguation_notes: MSV causes narrow, well-defined, broken yellow streaks parallel to leaf veins, unlike the diffuse mosaic patterns of MDMV.
recommended_action: Plant early in the season, use recommended MSV resistant varieties, eradicate grass weeds, control leafhopper vectors, keep fields free from grass weeds, remove residues of cereal crops, and catch vectors with sticky green traps.
confidence_source: CIMMYT Maize Diseases Guide p. 111; KALRO Disease Guide p. 27; KCEP-CRAL Maize Extension Manual p. 12
region_notes: Reported first from East Africa.

symptom_description: Stunting, shortened internodes; axillary bud development; excessive root branching; chloritic streaks at bases of leaves. Leaves appear crowded and erect.
trigger_conditions: Transmitted by leafhopper vectors.
disambiguation_notes: CSD causes excessive root branching and axillary bud development, distinguishing it from general virus chlorosis.
recommended_action: Control vectors, plant early, plant resistant varieties.
confidence_source: CIMMYT Maize Diseases Guide p. 112; KALRO Disease Guide p. 26
region_notes: Pl ease note that this disease has not yet been reported in Kenya and is therefore of quarantine importance.

symptom_description: Yellowing and stunting of the foliage. Can cause leaf mottling.
trigger_conditions: Transmitted by the maize aphid (Rhopalosiphum maidis).
recommended_action: Control aphid vectors.

symptom_description: Chlorotic streaks and mosaic patterns on the leaves.
trigger_conditions: Transmitted by mites. Associated as a potyvirus component in the MLN complex.
recommended_action: Control vectors and volunteer wheat crops.
confidence_source: CIMMYT Maize Diseases Guide p. 102; KALRO Disease Guide p. 7
region_notes: b) History of MLND in Kenya In K enya the first occurrence of unfamiliar maize disease was first reported in September 2011 in the low altitude zones of Bomet County (Longisa Division, 1900.

symptom_description: Infected plants develop a mosaic pattern and chlorotic streaks on leaves.
trigger_conditions: Transmitted by aphids. Serves as a major potyvirus partner in the MLND complex in Kenya.
recommended_action: Control aphid vectors.
region_notes: Seriously affects maize production in China.

symptom_description: Chlorotic spots and mosaic streaks on leaves, followed by necrosis.
trigger_conditions: Transmitted by wheat curl mites.
region_notes: Pl ease note that this disease has not yet been reported in Kenya and is therefore of quarantine importance.

symptom_description: First-instar larvae produce clusters of pinhole-type damage or small, round 'window panes' (transparent patches) on soft leaf tissues. Larger larvae make ragged, irregular elongated holes on leaves. Whorls show heavy feeding damage, with large amounts of moist, sawdust-like excreta (frass). Larvae can cut seedlings at base (similar to cutworms) and burrow into the whorl, growing point, and maize cobs, destroying seeds.
trigger_conditions: Moths are active at night during warm, humid evenings. Larvae develop between 11°C and 30°C. Rainfall can wash off young larvae, reducing populations.
disambiguation_notes: Larvae feel rough due to tiny spines on body. Head has a distinct, pale, upside-down Y-shaped mark (which cotton bollworm may also have but head is usually paler). Body has four raised spots in a square/trapezium on the eighth segment. Whorl damage is larger and leaves more frass than stem borers.
recommended_action: Monitoring and scouting (action threshold: 20% infestation in early whorl, 40% in late whorl). Hand-picking of caterpillars/eggs. Intercropping with legumes (beans, pigeon peas) or push-pull technology (intercrop with Desmodium and plant Napier grass as trap crop). Biological control with predators (ladybirds, hover flies) and parasites. Sprays of approved insecticides (e.g. Coragen 20SC, Prove 1.92EC, Match 50EC, Voliam Targo 063SC). Spray early morning/late evening, targeting top leaves and whorl.
confidence_source: FAO/CABI FAW Pocket Guide p. 4, 5, 8, 25; FAO FAW Manual p. 5, 6, 9
region_notes: Kenya-wide.

common_name: Maize Stem Borer / African Stalk Borer
symptom_description: Caterpillars feed on young plants causing 'dead hearts' (wilting and drying of the central leaf). They later burrow into stems, making tunnels that disrupt water and nutrient flow, leading to stunting, broken stalks, or lodging.
trigger_conditions: Aggravated by continuous maize cropping and crop residues on soil surface.
disambiguation_notes: FAW larvae feed primarily on leaves in whorl leaving massive frass before cob tunneling, whereas stem borers quickly tunnel into the stem. Stem borer caterpillars do not have the prominent Y-mark or rough skin spines of FAW.
recommended_action: Intercrop with non-host crops or green leaf desmodium. Plant trap crops (e.g., Napier grass) around the plot. Use biological control (predators and parasites). Apply recommended insecticides in whorl.
confidence_source: KALRO Disease Guide p. 9, 30; FAO/CABI FAW Pocket Guide p. 7; KCEP-CRAL Maize Extension Manual p. 10
region_notes: Western Region (Bungoma, Kakamega, Nandi, Trans Nzoia, Nakuru).

symptom_description: Larvae feed on leaves causing pinhole damage and then tunnel into the stem, leading to dead hearts or stem breakage.
trigger_conditions: Prevalent in warm, moist mid-altitude zones.
disambiguation_notes: Chilo partellus larvae are spotted, distinguishing them from the plain grey/pink larvae of Busseola fusca.
recommended_action: Intercrop with legumes or non-host crops, clean tillage, and use approved chemical insecticides.

symptom_description: Slender, pale green to yellow hoppers with two small black spots between the eyes that hop away when disturbed. Feed on plant sap, causing chlorosis and transmitting Maize Streak Virus.
trigger_conditions: Favored by dry weather and proximity to grasslands or previously irrigated grass crops.
disambiguation_notes: Hopper feeding causes minor direct damage, but they are primary vectors of Corn Streak Virus.
recommended_action: Plant early in the season, keep fields free from grass weeds, remove residues of cereal crops, and catch them with sticky green/yellow traps.
confidence_source: KALRO Disease Guide p. 27; KCEP-CRAL Maize Extension Manual p. 10

symptom_description: Small, soft-bodied blue-green insects colonizing the tassels and upper leaves. Feeding removes moisture and nutrients. Secretes sticky honeydew that covers leaves and tassels, leading to growth of sooty black mold. Leaves show yellow mottling, stunted growth, and dieback.
trigger_conditions: Prevalent during dry periods. Soft-bodied insects multiply rapidly under warm conditions.
disambiguation_notes: Colonies are found clustered inside the central leaf whorl or on tassels, producing honeydew.
recommended_action: Use mixed cropping, plant trap crops, encourage natural predators like ladybirds and hover flies, and spray with recommended insecticides in severe infestations.
confidence_source: KALRO Disease Guide p. 31; KCEP-CRAL Maize Extension Manual p. 10

symptom_description: Larvae feed on leaves, buds, growing points, flowers, and kernels. Reduces leaf area and slows plant growth; main damage is caused by feeding on flowers and kernels inside the cob.
trigger_conditions: Polyphagous pest that damages many crops. High populations are favored by warm weather.
disambiguation_notes: Bollworm caterpillars feel rough due to tiny spines, but their head is usually paler than FAW, and the Y-shaped mark is same color as head.
recommended_action: Intercrop maize with other crops, and spray with approved insecticides during heavy infestations.
confidence_source: KALRO Disease Guide p. 30; FAO/CABI FAW Pocket Guide p. 6; KCEP-CRAL Maize Extension Manual p. 10

symptom_description: Soil-dwelling caterpillars that attack young seedlings. They cut off the plant stem at or just below ground level, causing the seedling to collapse and dry up.
trigger_conditions: Common in soils with high organic residue or after weedy fallows.
disambiguation_notes: Cutworms cut plants cleanly at ground level and hide in the soil, unlike FAW which feeds primarily in the leaf whorl (though FAW can sometimes cut seedlings).
recommended_action: Seed dressing with approved chemicals, and spreading baits on the ground around seedlings.
confidence_source: KALRO Disease Guide p. 9; FAO FAW Manual p. 24; KCEP-CRAL Maize Extension Manual p. 11
region_notes: 9 g) Constraints in Maize farming in Kenya Maize is a very i mportant food security crop as well as cash crop for majority of farmers.

common_name: White Grubs / Chaffer Grubs / Larvae of Scarab Beetles
symptom_description: Larvae are white, slightly longer than an inch when fully grown, and curl into a 'C' shape. They eat plant roots, causing severe wilting where center leaves of young plants die. Can cause stunting or plant death.
trigger_conditions: Grubs have a 3-year life cycle. They can acquire MCMV from plant debris on soil surfaces and transmit it to young maize plants.
disambiguation_notes: Root feeding and C-shaped grub body distinguish this soil pest from foliar caterpillars.
recommended_action: Tillage to expose grubs to birds, and application of approved soil insecticides.
region_notes: OTHER MAIZE PESTS & DISEASES Topic Six: Factors affecting maize production in Kenya, Learning Objective: To gain knowl edge on other abiotic factors that contributes to MLND expression in maize field, Procedure: Lecture, slide shows Duration: 1 hr a) Field Pests Insect pests severely limit the production of maize, one of the most important cereal crops worldwide.

symptom_description: Minute, elongate, yellow-orange insects that feed deep in whorls, leaf sheaths, and lower leaf surfaces. Rasp leaf tissue and suck sap, creating a silvery cast on leaves and ear husks. Leaves distort, turn brown around edges, and cup upwards.
trigger_conditions: Feeding is only an economic problem on young seedlings (less than one foot tall) and at ear formation. Mechanical damage at ear formation provides entry for Fusarium ear rot.
disambiguation_notes: Minute size and silvery cast on leaves distinguish thrips from aphids or mites.
recommended_action: Spraying with approved insecticides, and maintaining plant vigor. Thrips are vectors that transmit MCMV.

symptom_description: Caterpillars feed on foliage and cobs, causing defoliation.
trigger_conditions: Warm and humid climates.
disambiguation_notes: Illustrated in pocket guide to distinguish from FAW (marked with ✘ as a lookalike).
recommended_action: Hand picking, application of chemical sprays if populations are high.

symptom_description: Larvae feed on leaves, creating small holes or skeletonizing them.
trigger_conditions: Favored by warm weather.
disambiguation_notes: Beet armyworm larvae are smaller and green/black, lacking the prominent head Y-mark of FAW.
recommended_action: Chemical sprays, promoting natural enemies.

symptom_description: Larvae appear in massive numbers (outbreaks) and rapidly defoliate whole fields, eating leaves down to the midrib.
trigger_conditions: Outbreaks often follow dry spells followed by heavy rains.
disambiguation_notes: African armyworm has a distinct black body with yellow stripes, and attacks in massive migrating populations (marching), whereas FAW is more solitary in whorls.
recommended_action: Monitoring outbreaks, spraying with recommended chemical insecticides.

symptom_description: Caterpillars feed on leaves and young shoots.
trigger_conditions: Warm, humid environments.
disambiguation_notes: Illustrated as a lookalike to FAW (marked with ✘ in pocket guide).
recommended_action: Approved chemical sprays.

symptom_description: A beetle-like insect that attacks maize on the cob, both before and after harvest. Adults bore into maize husks and cobs, producing large quantities of grain dust as they tunnel, hollow out kernels, and reduce them to dust.
trigger_conditions: Favored by poor storage conditions, high grain moisture, and late harvesting.
disambiguation_notes: Bores through husks and cobs producing massive amounts of wood/grain dust, which distinguishes it from the smaller maize weevils.
recommended_action: Early harvesting, drying below 13% moisture content, storage in cleaned and dusted stores/bags, use of hermetic bags (Agro-Z bags), metallic silos, or chemical treatment with Super Actellic @ 50g per 90kg bag.

symptom_description: Adults are small black beetles with a long, narrow snout. The female lays eggs inside the grain. The larva (grub) lives inside the grain, hollowing it out and leaving circular holes on the surface of the grain.
trigger_conditions: Favored by warm temperatures and grains stored at high moisture levels.
disambiguation_notes: Leaves distinct circular exit holes on the grain surface, smaller than the destruction caused by Larger Grain Borer.
recommended_action: Early harvesting, drying below 13% moisture, storing in clean and dusted store and bags, hermetic bags or metallic silos, and grain treatment with Super Actellic.

symptom_description: Makes the older leaves (the bottom portion of the maize plant) turn pale or yellowish-green. The deficiency then starts to create a V shape, starting at the tip of the leaf and running down the midrib. If not rectified, the deficiency works its way up the plant from older (lower) to newer leaves. The stalks tend to be thin and spindly.
trigger_conditions: Develops commonly in wet to saturated soils or under cool soil temperatures. N can leach out under heavy rainfall in light-textured (sandy) soils, or can be denitrified in flooded soils. Can be induced after midseason when soils tend to be dry, or in soils with large amounts of low-nitrogen-containing residues.
disambiguation_notes: Nitrogen deficiency yellowing starts on older leaves and forms a V-shape down the midrib, whereas Sulfur deficiency causes a general yellowing that is more visible on newer leaves.
recommended_action: Apply nitrogenous fertilizers (like CAN top-dressing at 92kg/acre when knee-high, or urea), and add organic manure.

symptom_description: Causes a distinct dark green color with reddish to purplish leaf margins, typically starting from the tip of the older leaves. Stunted growth is also typical. Symptoms normally disappear by the time the plant is waist-high.
trigger_conditions: Since P is fairly immobile in soil, any soil condition that limits root growth (cool temperature, wet or very dry conditions, compaction) can induce the deficiency. Acid soils fix phosphorus, making it unavailable.
disambiguation_notes: Reddish-purple margins on older leaves, disappearing as the plant grows waist-high. Some hybrids show purple colors even when P is not deficient.
recommended_action: Apply basal phosphatic fertilizers (like DAP at 50kg/acre at planting), and manage soil acidity using lime or fertilizers with a liming effect (MEA Mazao, Mavuno basal).
region_notes: High deficiency symptoms observed in lower Eastern region of Kenya.

symptom_description: Observed as yellowing and necrosis (death) of the edge of older leaves, starting from the tip. When the problem persists, this deficiency will continue to move up from older to newer leaves, while the top leaves may look completely green. Stalks are thin and not strong, causing lodging of the crop later in the season.
trigger_conditions: Soil conditions that restrict root growth can induce deficiency, especially at early stages when the root system is small. Soils with low K buffer capacity (sandy soils) can cause the deficiency.
disambiguation_notes: Yellowing and necrosis are restricted to the edges (margins) of older leaves, unlike Nitrogen deficiency which yellowing is V-shaped down the midrib.
recommended_action: Apply potassium-containing fertilizers (NPK) according to soil test recommendations.

symptom_description: Appears in lower leaves as yellow or white streaking between veins (interveinal chlorosis). The leaves eventually become reddish-purple, and the edge and tip die if the deficiency is severe.
trigger_conditions: Acidic and sandy soils are most likely to be deficient in Mg.
disambiguation_notes: Characterized by white/yellow striping between veins on lower leaves, which eventually turn reddish-purple.
recommended_action: Apply magnesium-rich fertilizers or dolomitic limestone to correct soil acidity and supply magnesium.

symptom_description: Causes a general yellowing of the foliage, tending to be more visible in the newer leaves.
trigger_conditions: Typically observed in soils with low organic matter (including sandy soils), low pH, and cold, wet conditions that reduce mineralization of S from organic matter.
disambiguation_notes: Since S is not easily translocated, deficiency tends to be more visible in the newer leaves, as opposed to N deficiency which is more pronounced in older leaves.
recommended_action: Apply sulfur-containing fertilizers (e.g. ammonium sulfate or gypsum). Grains will often recover once the root system reaches the S in the subsurface soil.

symptom_description: Appears between veins as light green to white stripes or as wide bands starting at the base of the leaf and extending toward the tip of the newer leaves. The edge of the leaf as well as the midrib usually stays green. In cases of severe deficiency, new leaves are almost white.
trigger_conditions: Most commonly observed in soils low in organic matter, sandy soils with high pH (>7.3), and cool, wet soils.
disambiguation_notes: Wide white/light green bands at the leaf base on newer leaves, with leaf edges and midrib remaining green. In severe cases, the entire leaf emerges white (white bud).
recommended_action: Apply zinc sulfate or other zinc chelates as soil amendments or foliar sprays.

symptom_description: Interveinal chlorosis (yellowing between veins) on newer leaves, where veins remain green. In severe cases, leaves turn completely pale or white.
trigger_conditions: Most common in soils containing calcium carbonate (alkaline/calcareous soils) or under high soil pH.
disambiguation_notes: Yellowing between veins on the youngest leaves, unlike Magnesium deficiency which occurs on older leaves.
recommended_action: Apply foliar iron sprays or iron chelates to the soil.

symptom_description: Interveinal chlorosis on newer leaves, similar to iron deficiency, but lesions can develop olive-green to grey specks or stripes.
trigger_conditions: Most common in soils containing calcium carbonate (alkaline/calcareous soils) or poorly drained organic soils.
disambiguation_notes: Chlorosis is on newer leaves, often accompanied by olive-green/grey specks, distinguishing it from general nitrogen chlorosis.
recommended_action: Apply manganese sulfate or manganese chelates.

symptom_description: If maize stands in water for more than two days, it will wither and die off.
trigger_conditions: Waterlogged soils, poorly drained soils, or heavy flooding.
disambiguation_notes: Causes rapid wilting and death, unlike drought which causes leaves to roll first and slowly wither.
recommended_action: Avoid waterlogged soils. Ensure soils are well drained and well aerated.

symptom_description: Causes leaves to roll and plants to wilt. If drought occurs at flowering time, it will interfere with pollination and drastically lower the yields.
trigger_conditions: Erratic rainfall and poor distribution during the growing period, especially during the first five weeks after sowing and at flowering.
disambiguation_notes: Causes leaves to roll tightly along the midrib to reduce water loss.
recommended_action: Plant within the first two weeks of the onset of rains. Enhance crop water conservation.

symptom_description: Causes stunted growth, poor root development, and induces nutrient deficiencies (such as phosphorus and magnesium deficiencies).
trigger_conditions: Highly weathered soils, continuous cropping, or leaching under high rainfall. Strongly acidic soils (pH < 5.0).
disambiguation_notes: Soil acidity limits phosphorus solubility, inducing typical purple leaf margin symptoms.
recommended_action: Liming is recommended for acid soils. Use fertilizers with a liming effect like MEA Mazao (100 kg/acre), Mavuno basal (100 kg/acre), and Mavuno for topdressing (75 kg/acre).
confidence_source: KALRO Disease Guide p. 33; KCEP-CRAL Maize Extension Manual p. 9

symptom_description: Restricts root growth, leading to stunted plants and inducing nutrient deficiencies.
trigger_conditions: Use of heavy farm machinery under wet soil conditions, or lack of deep tillage.
disambiguation_notes: Limits the plant's small root system, making it unable to absorb immobile nutrients like Phosphorus.
recommended_action: Deep tillage/ploughing to break the hardpan.

symptom_description: Extends the life cycle of the crop (longer maturity period). Can result in poor germination and stunted early growth.
trigger_conditions: High altitudes or planting during cool/cold seasons.
disambiguation_notes: Extends the vegetative growth stage.
recommended_action: Select adapted varieties for highland zones (e.g. H6213, H6210 which mature in 160-210 days).
region_notes: Highland zones (Trans Nzoia, Nandi, Nakuru, Kakamega, Bungoma).

symptom_description: Exposes the crop to excessive respiration and lowers yields. Accelerates water loss.
trigger_conditions: Low altitudes or hot, dry weather conditions.
disambiguation_notes: Often occurs in combination with water stress.
recommended_action: Select adapted drought-tolerant or early-maturing varieties.
region_notes: Moist mid-altitude or dry land zones.

symptom_description: Causes freezing and death of plant tissues. Leaves turn brown and dry up rapidly.
trigger_conditions: Temperatures falling below freezing point.
disambiguation_notes: Frost damage is sudden and uniform across the canopy, unlike diseases.
recommended_action: Avoid planting in frost-prone areas or select resistant varieties.

symptom_description: Non-infectious spots that appear on leaves. These can be chlorotic or necrotic spots, often appearing uniformly across the leaf blade.
trigger_conditions: Genetically controlled or physiological response, non-infectious.
disambiguation_notes: Easily confused with eyespot of maize (Kabatiella zeae) or early spotting induced by Curvularia.
recommended_action: Confirm deficiency or pathogen presence via laboratory analysis before treatment.

symptom_description: Damage or wounds on stalks, leaves, or kernels. Provides entry points for pathogens.
trigger_conditions: Farming operations, hail, wind, or feeding by insects like thrips or birds.
disambiguation_notes: Physical cuts/scars on the plant tissue, which later rot.
recommended_action: Avoid injuring the plants during mechanical operations. Control insects like thrips that damage developing kernels.
confidence_source: KALRO Disease Guide p. 22; KCEP-CRAL Maize Extension Manual p. 12

symptom_description: If maize is planted in very low or very high altitudes that are outside its recommended zone, poor yields will be realized.
trigger_conditions: Planting varieties outside their recommended agro-ecological altitudes.
disambiguation_notes: Causes poor growth, small ears, and low yield due to climate mismatch.
recommended_action: Select appropriate maize varieties recommended for the specific altitude zone (e.g. H6213 for highlands, WH509 for mid-altitude).
region_notes: Western Region implementing counties.
